title: The Glove and the Lions
author: Leigh Hunt
tagline: Narrative poem · a royal lion fight · vanity, courage and true love

sourceNote.thirdParty: "The Glove and the Lions" is a poem by Leigh Hunt, first published in the nineteenth century and now in the public domain in most countries. The poem is not reproduced or quoted here. Read it in your prescribed textbook.
sourceNote.boardprep: The paraphrase, notes on theme, tone and devices, vocabulary and all questions and answers on this page were written by BoardPrep as original study material and are not taken from any textbook or guide.

overview.intro: King Francis and his court are watching a fight between lions, a cruel entertainment of the age. A lady of the court, wishing to test how much her lover loves her, drops her glove into the arena among the fighting beasts. She expects the knight to risk his life to fetch it. He does exactly that, walks calmly among the lions, picks up the glove, returns, and throws it in her face. He has proved his courage, but he has also shown her what he thinks of her. The king agrees that the lady had acted out of vanity and not out of love.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: Narrative poem in rhymed verse, telling a story from beginning to end

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: The court of King Francis, at a lion fight held for the entertainment of the nobles

facts.label: Main characters
facts.value: The king, the lady, and the knight De Lorge

facts.label: Theme
facts.value: Vanity against true love; courage; the cruelty of testing another person's life

facts.label: Tone
facts.value: Lively and dramatic in the story, ironic and moral at the close

learn.title: What the poem says, stage by stage

items: Stage 1 (the setting): King Francis sits with his lords and ladies to enjoy a spectacle of lions fighting. The court watches with interest, as if at a sport.
Stage 2 (the fight): the lions roar and struggle, tearing at one another. The onlookers are fascinated by the display of animal strength and danger.

Stage 3 (the lady's test): a lady of the court, wanting to prove her lover's devotion, lets her glove fall into the arena among the lions. She then invites him, by look or word, to bring it back if he truly loves her.
Stage 4 (the knight's act): the knight, De Lorge, bows, goes down into the arena, and calmly picks up the glove even though the lions are fierce and close. He then returns safely to the gallery.

Stage 5 (the reply): instead of handing over the glove with a bow, he throws it in the lady's face. He shows that he did not do it for love of her, and he rejects a person who would put his life at risk for a whim.
Stage 6 (the king's verdict): the court is stunned. King Francis remarks that the lady acted from vanity, not love, and that the knight was right in what he did.

items.meaning: Proud and vain. She treats her lover's life as something to be tested for her own satisfaction, showing that she cares more for admiration than for him.
Brave, calm and self-respecting. He does not refuse the dangerous task, but he answers her selfishness with a public rebuke instead of loving thanks.
The royal spectator, who watches cruel entertainment but shows sound judgement when he names the lady's motive as vanity.
Symbols of raw danger and cruelty. They also represent the risks that the court takes lightly when it treats life as a show.

blocks.text: Love cannot be tested by putting the beloved in danger. A person who plays games with another's life is vain, and not loving. True courage includes the courage to refuse to be treated as a prize or a plaything, and the knight shows this by going down among the lions and then rejecting the lady.
Secondary ideas: the cruelty of entertainments that use suffering as a spectacle, and the contrast between outward show at court and real feeling.

items: The opening has a lively, story-telling tone, drawing the reader into the scene of the royal spectacle.
The mood grows tense as the glove falls and the knight goes down among the lions.
The tone at the end is ironic and moral. The poet does not scold the lady; he lets the knight's action and the king's remark deliver the judgement.

items.meaning: The poem follows a clear line from setting to test, action, surprise and verdict, so it reads like a short story in verse.
The lady expects to be proved lovable by her knight's courage, but the result is that she is publicly shamed. The man who does the brave thing is the one who ends the relationship.
Scenes of roaring, fighting lions create a vivid, loud, dangerous picture that contrasts with the court's calm enjoyment.
The rich, comfortable court set beside the bloody arena; the lady's vanity beside the knight's dignity; the crowd's excitement beside the knight's calmness.
Rhymed verse with a brisk rhythm moves the story quickly, which suits its dramatic and surprising ending.
The glove stands for the lady's vanity and for the test that is really a game; throwing it back is the knight's refusal to play.

items: Tell the story in sequence, but do not spend the whole answer on plot. Add a comment on what each event shows.
The knight is brave, but the point is not that he wins her. He rejects her. Do not say that he does it to win her love.
Use the king's remark as evidence of the moral. It shows that even an onlooker sees the lady's motive.
For irony questions, always state what was expected and what actually happened.

keyPoints: King Francis and his court watch a lion fight for entertainment.
A lady drops her glove into the arena to test her lover's courage.
The knight De Lorge retrieves it and throws it in her face.
The king remarks that the lady acted from vanity and not from love.
The poem shows that love should not be tested by risking a life for a whim.
The ending is ironic: the brave act ends the relationship.
examFocus: Narrate the incident of the glove and explain its meaning.
Character sketches of the lady and of De Lorge.
Why does the knight throw the glove in the lady's face?
The king's remark and what it shows about the lady's motive.
Whether the lady's test was fair, and what true love should look like.

questions.prompt: Why does the lady drop her glove into the arena?
options: It slips from her hand by accident
She wants to test whether her lover will risk his life for her
She wants to stop the lion fight
She hopes to give the glove to the king
questions.answer: She wants to test whether her lover will risk his life for her.
questions.explanation: The glove is dropped on purpose, as a test of the knight's courage and devotion.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the glove falls by accident.

questions.prompt: What does the knight do after he brings back the glove?
options: He kneels and gives it to her lovingly
He gives it to the king
He throws it in the lady's face
He puts it back in the arena
questions.answer: He throws it in the lady's face.
questions.explanation: This act shows that he despises her test and that he did not do it for love of her.
questions.commonMistake: Expecting a romantic ending. The poem is a satire on vanity.

questions.prompt: What does the king conclude about the lady's motive?
options: She acted out of vanity, not love
She acted out of fear of the lions
She acted to please the court
She acted out of anger with the knight
questions.answer: She acted out of vanity, not love.
questions.explanation: The king's verdict states the moral of the poem: a test that endangers a life for show is vanity, not love.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the king's verdict with the knight's own words.

questions.prompt: Describe the scene at King Francis's court at the beginning of the poem.
questions.answer: King Francis is sitting with his lords and ladies, and the court has gathered to watch a fight between lions. The nobles look on with interest, treating the dangerous struggle as an entertainment, and the scene is one of ease and display above a violent arena.
questions.explanation: Mention the king and court, the lion fight, and the attitude of the spectators.
questions.commonMistake: Describing a battle between soldiers. It is a contest between animals for the court's amusement.

questions.prompt: Why does De Lorge throw the glove in the lady's face after bringing it back?
questions.answer: De Lorge understands that the lady was not thinking of his safety at all. She wanted to test and display his devotion, and she was willing to risk his life for it. By throwing the glove back he shows her that he sees her vanity, and that he will not be treated as a plaything. His brave act is thus also a sharp rebuke and the end of their attachment.
questions.explanation: Give his understanding, her fault, and the meaning of the gesture.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that he throws it in anger at the lions or the king.

questions.prompt: Write a character sketch of the lady in 'The Glove and the Lions'.
questions.answer: The lady is proud, vain and thoughtless. She is more interested in being admired than in the safety of the man who loves her, and she treats his life as something to test for her own satisfaction. She is also attention-seeking, since she stages her test in front of the whole court. She lacks empathy, as she never seems to think of the danger to him. By the end, her behaviour is exposed by the knight's action and the king's remark, and she is humiliated in public.
questions.explanation: Choose three or four qualities and link them to what she does. Mention the outcome for her.
questions.commonMistake: Describing her as a loving and loyal person who was unlucky.

questions.prompt: Explain the irony in the ending of the poem.
questions.answer: The lady expects the knight's brave deed to prove his love and to increase her own pride. Instead the deed ends the relationship, because he uses it to reject her in public. The man who takes the greatest risk is the one who walks away, and the woman who set the test is the one who is shamed. The irony lies in the gap between what she wanted, a triumph, and what she got, a rebuke that the king himself approves.
questions.explanation: State the expectation, the actual result, and the effect on the lady.
questions.commonMistake: Retelling the ending without saying what makes it ironic.

questions.prompt: 'The Glove and the Lions' is a poem about the difference between vanity and true love. Discuss.
questions.answer: The poem sets the lady's behaviour beside the knight's. The lady wants proof that others admire her, and she is willing to risk the life of her lover to obtain it. That is vanity: it puts self-display above the person she claims to love. True love, by contrast, would never place the beloved in danger for a whim, and would value his life over any proof of devotion. The knight shows courage by going into the arena, but he shows self-respect and a clearer understanding of love by rejecting the test. The king's remark confirms this reading. The poem therefore teaches that love is shown through care and respect, not through dangerous tests, and that vanity destroys the thing it claims to want.
questions.explanation: Define vanity and love through the characters, use the knight's action and the king's verdict as evidence, and conclude with the moral.
questions.commonMistake: Praising the knight's courage alone and forgetting the lady's motive.

questions.prompt: Do you think the knight was right to accept the lady's challenge and then to reject her? Give reasons for your view.
questions.answer: The knight was right to reject her but questionable in accepting the test. Going among the lions risked his life to satisfy someone who did not deserve it, and a wiser person might have refused at once. However, his calm courage and his later action show that he acted with a clear purpose: he needed to see the lady's true nature, and having seen it, he made his answer plain in a way that everyone could understand. Some readers may say a private conversation would have been kinder. Yet the test was public, and the rebuke was a fair reply to a public humiliation. On balance, I think the rejection was justified, and the risk was unwise but understandable in a knight of that age.
questions.explanation: Any consistent view is accepted. Look for a clear position, reference to the poem, and awareness of the other side.
questions.commonMistake: Answering only with what happens in the poem and giving no judgement.

questions.prompt: What does the glove symbolise in the poem, and why is the knight's act of throwing it back important?
questions.answer: The glove symbolises the lady's vanity and the game she plays with the knight's life. It is a small object that carries a large and dangerous test. When the knight throws it back, he refuses to take part in the game and returns her vanity to her in the most public way. The act is important because it turns the glove from a token of love into a sign of her disgrace.
questions.explanation: State what the glove stands for, and connect the throwing back to the theme.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the glove as only an accessory in the story.
